fixes.current: Albania's communist government dotted the country with small concrete bunkers from 1967 to 1986, an average of about 5.7 for every square kilometer.
fixes.value: Albania's communist government built well over 100,000 small concrete bunkers from the 1960s to the 1980s, and many of them still stand across the country.
fixes.reason: The 5.7 per square kilometer figure is unreliable: the same Wikipedia lead pairs it with 'more than 750,000 bunkers' (about 26 per km2 over 28,748 km2), while the state-archive count of 173,371 bunkers by 1983 gives about 6.0 per km2; no estimate yields 5.7, so the app ships a precise statistic that no source supports. Construction dates also differ between sources (1967-1986 in Wikipedia's infobox and body; 1975-1983 for the main program per Bunk'Art and Euronews). The replacement states only what every estimate supports: well over 100,000 bunkers, 1960s to 1980s, many still standing. 155 characters, one sentence, neutral, no year-stamped statistic, true in five years. Both verifiers independently reached the same conclusion.

fixes.current: Albania's flag is plain red with a black two-headed eagle. The eagle comes from the seal of Skanderbeg's Kastrioti family, who fought the Ottomans in the 1400s; two-headed eagles were also a Byzantine imperial symbol. Ismail Qemali raised this flag when he declared independence on 28 November 1912. The 2002 flag law only describes the design; red is often said to mean bravery and blood shed for freedom, but no law says so.
fixes.value: Albania's flag is plain red with a black two-headed eagle. The eagle comes from the coat of arms of Skanderbeg's Kastrioti family, who fought the Ottomans in the 1400s; two-headed eagles were also a Byzantine imperial symbol. Ismail Qemali raised a red flag with the eagle when he declared independence on 28 November 1912. Red is often said to mean bravery and blood shed for freedom, but the 2002 flag law gives no meaning.
fixes.reason: Two claims overstate the sources. (1) Wikipedia's Flag of Albania never says 'seal'; it says 'The Kastrioti's coat of arms, depicting a black double-headed eagle on a red field'. (2) It states 'there is no trace evidence of the original flag that was raised in Vlorë on 28 November 1912', so 'raised this flag' (meaning the exact current design) is too strong; the safe claim, supported by the memoir account it cites, is a red flag with the eagle. The law sentence is reworded to the confirmed facts: Law 8926 of 2002 defines design, ratio and colors and gives no meaning; the red meaning is unattributed prose on Wikipedia, so it stays hedged. 425 characters, one paragraph, no flag jargon, no double quotes, American spelling. Both verifiers flagged the same two issues.

fixes.current: Andorra's flag has blue, yellow and red upright bands with the coat of arms in the middle. Adopted in 1866, it is often said to mix the blue and red of France with the yellow and red of Catalonia and Spain. On the shield, a bishop's hat and staff stand for the Bishop of Urgell, the red stripes for Foix and Catalonia, and the two cows for Béarn, all old powers over Andorra. The motto means united virtue is stronger; a 1996 law fixed the design.
fixes.value: Andorra's flag has blue, yellow and red bands with the coat of arms in the middle. Said to date from 1866, its colors are often linked to France (blue and red) and to Catalonia and Spain (yellow and red). On the shield, a bishop's hat and staff stand for the Bishop of Urgell, the red stripes for Foix and Catalonia, and the two cows for Béarn, all tied to Andorra's history. The motto means united virtue is stronger; a 1996 law set the design.
fixes.reason: (1) 'Adopted in 1866' is stated as fact, but Britannica says 'The national flag is said to date from 1866, but the first legal authority for it is unknown', and Wikipedia attributes the date only traditionally (Napoleon III), so it must be hedged. (2) 'All old powers over Andorra' is wrong for the lower quarters: the Coat of arms of Andorra article describes the top quarters (Bishop of Urgell, Count of Foix) as the 'two traditional protectors' and the bottom quarters (Catalonia, Béarn) as 'territories that Andorra has historically been reliant upon', not rulers of it. 'All tied to Andorra's history' is accurate for all four. Britannica confirms the motto as 'Strength united is stronger' and the colors as only possibly influenced by France and Spain, matching the hedged wording. 445 characters (the old text was 447, so 'upright' is dropped to make room), no jargon, no double quotes, American spelling.

fixes.current: Bosnia's parliament could not agree on a flag, so on 4 February 1998 High Representative Carlos Westendorp imposed this design by Mladen Kolobarić; its blue and yellow match the Council of Europe flag. The triangle's three corners are usually read as the three main peoples, Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, and its shape as the country's outline. The white stars are usually read as Europe, running off the edges to suggest an endless row.
fixes.value: Bosnia and Herzegovina's parliament could not agree on a flag, so on 4 February 1998 the international peace envoy Carlos Westendorp imposed this design by Mladen Kolobarić. His office said the triangle stands for the three main peoples, Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, the yellow for the sun and hope, and the blue and the stars for Europe; the stars run off the edges to suggest an endless row. The blue and yellow match the Council of Europe flag.
fixes.reason: The meanings were given officially when the flag was announced, so they should be stated plainly with attribution rather than hedged as 'usually read'. The flags-of-the-world page quotes the Office of the High Representative's spokesman on 4 February 1998: 'The triangle represents the three constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the yellow the sun representing the symbol of hope. The blue and the stars represent Europe'. The current text omits the stated meaning of the yellow entirely. Because the quote came from the office's spokesman, not Westendorp personally, the replacement says 'His office said' rather than 'He said' as the verifier proposed. 'High Representative' is replaced by a plain-English description for a 10-year-old. The 'country outline' reading (cited by Wikipedia to the CIA Factbook) is dropped in favor of the official explanation. The failure of parliament, the date and the Council of Europe colors were confirmed by the verifiers against the OHR decision; the flags-of-the-world page also confirms the colors were changed to match the Council of Europe. 446 characters, no double quotes, American spelling, no jargon. The designer's name is kept as shipped (see doubts).

The field rule names Wikipedia's list of countries by area as the source; I opened that list and its Malta row gives 315 km2 total (315 land, 0 inland water, note cu). The app's 316 was taken from the Malta article infobox only because the list fetch was truncated in the first pass.

fixes.current: Kosovo's flag was adopted on 17 February 2008, the day it declared independence from Serbia. It won a design competition held under UN-led talks, whose rules said the flag must show all of Kosovo's peoples and avoid Albanian or Serbian symbols like the double-headed eagle. The gold shape is a map of the country on blue. The six white stars stand for Kosovo's six main communities: Albanians, Serbs, Bosniaks, Turks, Roma and Gorani.
fixes.value: Kosovo's flag dates from 17 February 2008, the day it declared independence. It won a competition run by Kosovo's institutions during UN-led talks, which required symbols for all its peoples, not one group. The gold shape is a map of the country; its designer said blue stands for a wish to join Europe and the West, gold for Kosovo's wealth. The six white stars are its six main communities: Albanians, Serbs, Bosniaks, Turks, Roma and Gorani.
fixes.reason: Two confirmed problems with the current text: (1) the competition was organized by the Kosovo Unity Team, an informal group from Kosovo's Provisional Institutions of Self-Government, not held under the UN talks themselves (Wikipedia: the UN talks only set the terms the symbols had to meet); (2) the text gives no account of the blue and gold, while Britannica records the designer Muhamer Ibrahimi's stated meanings (blue for Kosovo's aspirations toward Euro-Atlantic institutions, gold for its prosperity), which the replacement states as the designer's claim in plain words. The replacement is 444 characters, one paragraph, no double quotes, no jargon, and keeps the six-communities sentence confirmed by Wikipedia.

fixes.current: Malta's flag is white by the pole and red outside, as its 1964 independence constitution requires. A legend credits Count Roger of Sicily with the colors in 1091, but historians call it a myth; they more likely come from the Knights of St John's white cross on red. The George Cross, edged in red, in the upper left corner was given by King George VI in 1942 for Malta's bravery under heavy bombing in World War II; it joined the flag in 1943.
fixes.value: Malta's flag is white by the pole and red outside, as its 1964 constitution requires. A legend credits Count Roger of Sicily with the colors in 1091, but it is unproven and often called a myth; they more likely come from the Knights of St John's white cross on red. The George Cross, edged in red, in the upper left corner was given by King George VI in 1942 for Malta's bravery under heavy bombing in World War II; it joined the flag in 1943.
fixes.reason: The phrase 'historians call it a myth' attributes the debunking to historians, which neither source supports: Wikipedia's 'debunked as a 19th-century myth' line cites WorldAtlas, and the same article notes Mdina linked its colors to Roger in the late Middle Ages (Gaul 2007); Britannica only calls the legend 'unsubstantiated'. The field rule requires traditional readings to be hedged, so the replacement says the legend is unproven and often called a myth. All other claims (constitution wording, George Cross awarded by George VI on 15 April 1942, added 28 December 1943, red edge from 21 September 1964) were confirmed in both sources. Replacement is 443 characters, one paragraph, no double quotes.

fixes.current: After the 1910 revolution ended the monarchy, the flag became law in 1911. Green and red were the republicans' colors, often said to mean hope and blood shed for Portugal. The yellow armillary sphere was King Manuel I's emblem in the Age of Discoveries. The five small blue shields date from the 1100s; the tale of a 1139 battle is a myth. The seven castles on the red border are often tied to the Algarve conquest, but their origin is unclear.
fixes.value: The flag became law in 1911 after a 1910 revolution ended the monarchy. Green and red were republican colors, often said to mean hope and blood shed for Portugal. The yellow armillary sphere was King Manuel I's emblem in the Age of Discoveries. The five blue shields date from the 1100s; the tale of five Moorish kings beaten in 1139 is a myth. The seven castles on the red border are often tied to the Algarve conquest; their origin is unclear.
fixes.reason: The current sentence 'the tale of a 1139 battle is a myth' reads as if the Battle of Ourique never happened; the battle (25 July 1139, Afonso Henriques against Almoravid forces) is historical. What the Wikipedia flag article calls 'pure myth' is the legend, first written down in 1419, that the five shields commemorate five Moorish kings killed there and Christ's wounds. The replacement names the legend as the myth, keeps the yellow sphere and every other claim, and is 449 characters. [Edited after review: "often read as" is not one of the reason phrases the dataset test looks for; "often said to mean" is, and says the same.]

fixes.current: Adopted in 2004, the flag is based on the royal banner of King Nikola I: red with a gold border and the coat of arms. The two-headed eagle, a symbol of Byzantine origin, was used by the Crnojević rulers in the 1400s and is often read as church and state united. Its crown, scepter and orb copy Russian imperial arms. Prince-Bishop Sava added the lion shield in the 1700s as a sign of church authority. The law gives the colors no meaning.
fixes.value: Adopted in 2004, the flag is based on the royal banner of King Nikola I: red with a gold border and the coat of arms. The two-headed eagle, a symbol of Byzantine origin, was used by the Crnojević rulers in the 1400s and is often read as church and state united. Its crown, scepter and orb copy Russian imperial arms. Prince-Bishop Sava added the lion in the 1700s as a sign of church authority. The law gives the colors no meaning.
fixes.reason: The Wikipedia coat-of-arms article says vladika Sava removed the family arms from the eagle's breast and added a golden lion passant below the eagle; the lion was placed on the blue-and-green shield on the eagle's chest only under Prince Danilo in the 1800s. Saying Sava 'added the lion shield' credits him with a placement he did not make; dropping 'shield' keeps the sentence accurate at 431 characters.

fixes.reason: The shipped flag image (app/src/main/res/drawable-nodpi/flag_va.webp) shows one gold key and one silver key crossed and bound by a red cord; the coat of arms is defined by law as having a silver key and a gold key, and the flag article says the yellow and white halves took their colours from the gold and silver of the keys. fixes.current: Blue and red were the colors of the prince's household uniforms from 1764, and the 1921 constitution made the blue over red flag official. At the 1936 Olympics Liechtenstein found Haiti's flag looked exactly the same, so in 1937 a gold crown was added in the upper left corner. The government said blue stands for the sky, red for evening fires in people's homes, and the crown for the unity of people and prince. Its shape was updated in 1982.
fixes.value: Blue and red were the colors of the prince's household uniforms from 1764, and the 1921 constitution made the blue over red flag official. At the 1936 Olympics Liechtenstein found Haiti's flag was identical, so in 1937 a gold crown was added in the upper left corner. The government said blue stands for the sky, red for evening fires in people's homes, and the crown for the unity of people and prince. The crown's shape was updated in 1982.
fixes.reason: The closing sentence 'Its shape was updated in 1982' has an unclear referent and can be read as the flag's shape changing; the Flag of Liechtenstein article (opened) states 'A design with a modified crown was adopted on 30 June 1982', so it was the crown that changed. The replacement names the crown explicitly, trims one phrase to stay in range (442 characters, counted), and keeps every other fact, all of which I re-confirmed: 1764 colors under Prince Joseph Wenzel I, 1921 constitution giving official status, 1936 Olympics clash with Haiti, crown adopted 24 June 1937, Hoop's sky / evening fires / unity explanation (Flag Institute).

fixes.current: The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with its colors reversed, adopted in 1864 as a tribute to Switzerland, where the movement was founded.
fixes.value: The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with its colors reversed; the 1906 Geneva Convention says this honors Switzerland, where the movement was founded.
fixes.reason: The tribute motive is stated as settled fact tied to 1864, but the 1864 Convention text (Article 7) only prescribes a red cross on a white ground with no mention of Switzerland; the respect-for-Switzerland wording and the reversal of the federal colours were first written into Article 18 of the 1906 revision, and Red Cross historian Pierre Boissier found no clear evidence that this was the original intention. The replacement (153 characters) attributes the honor reading to its documented source and drops the contested year.

fixes.current: White and red come from the coat of arms of Bohemia, a white lion on a red shield, and were Czechoslovakia's colors from 1918. Because that two-band flag looked like Poland's, Jaroslav Kursa added a blue triangle on the flagpole side in 1920; blue is a color of Moravia and Slovakia. When Czechoslovakia split in 1993 the Czech Republic kept the flag. No law gives the colors a meaning; they are often read as Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia.
fixes.value: White and red come from the coat of arms of Bohemia, a white lion on a red shield, and were Czechoslovakia's colors from 1918. Because that flag looked like Poland's, Jaroslav Kursa added a blue triangle on the flagpole side in 1920, the blue standing for Slovakia. After the 1993 split the Czech Republic kept the flag. No law gives the colors a meaning; white is often linked to Bohemia, red to Moravia and blue to fairness and independence.
fixes.reason: Re-opened both sources: the Wikipedia flag article says the triangle was added because the white-red flag was almost identical to Poland's, names Kursa, and states blue used to symbolize Slovakia (now impartiality and sovereignty), white Bohemia and red Moravia; Britannica says the blue referenced the Slovak (and Ruthenian) colors. Neither gives Moravia as the reason for the blue, so the shipped sentence ties blue to Moravia and then implies red is Moravia in the last clause, which is inconsistent with the sourced readings. Replacement keeps the hedging, has no jargon or double quotes, and is 443 characters (counted).

fixes.current: Moldova's flag uses the blue, yellow and red of neighboring Romania, with which it shares a language and history. It was adopted in 1990 as Moldova moved toward independence from the Soviet Union. In the center an eagle holds a cross in its beak, an olive branch read as peace and a scepter for power; its shield shows an aurochs head, emblem of medieval Moldavia, with a star, a rose and a crescent. No official meaning is given for the colors.
fixes.value: Moldova's flag uses the blue, yellow and red of neighboring Romania, with which it shares a language and history. It was adopted in 1990 as Moldova moved toward independence. In the center an eagle holds a cross in its beak, an olive branch often read as peace, and a scepter; its shield shows an aurochs head, emblem of medieval Moldavia, with a star, a rose and a crescent. No official meaning is given for the colors or the scepter.
fixes.reason: The current text states as fact that the scepter stands for power. I re-opened the Coat of arms of Moldova article (which quotes the arms law, Law No. 32 of 2013, Art. 2) and the Flag of Moldova article: the law only lists the objects the eagle holds (cross, olive branch, scepter) and neither article gives any meaning for the scepter; Wikipedia says only that the olive branch symbolizes peace. The field rule requires an unexplained feature to be said so rather than given an invented meaning. Replacement is 435 characters, one paragraph, no jargon.

fixes.current: White, blue and red bands with the coat of arms near the pole. Slovaks adopted these Pan-Slavic colors in 1848. The arms were added in 1992 so the flag would not match Russia's. On its red shield a white double cross stands on three blue hills: the hills are traditionally read as the Tatra, Fatra and Matra mountains, and the cross is a Christian symbol often linked to the missionaries Cyril and Methodius. The law gives the colors no meaning.
fixes.value: White, blue and red bands with the coat of arms near the pole. Slovaks took up these Pan-Slavic colors, modeled on Russia's flag, in 1848; the arms were added in 1992 so the flag would not match Russia's. On the red shield a white double cross stands on three blue hills: the hills are traditionally read as the Tatra, Fatra and Matra ranges, and the cross is a Christian symbol often tied to Cyril and Methodius. The law gives the colors no meaning.
fixes.reason: The field rule asks that a shared motif (Pan-Slavic colors) name its shared origin in one clause; the current text names the motif but not the origin. Confirmed in two opened sources: Wikipedia's flag article says the 1848 Slovak design was inspired by the flag of Russia, and Britannica says white, blue and red were recognized as Pan-Slavic colors because Russia had chosen them for its flag. All other claims (1848, arms added 3 September 1992 because the plain bands matched Russia's flag, Tatra/Fatra/Matra as a 16th-century tradition, Cyril and Methodius hedged, no official color meaning) hold against both sources. Replacement is exactly 450 characters, one paragraph, American spelling, no jargon.

fixes.current: Estonia's flag has three equal bands of blue, black and white, colors chosen by the Estonian Students' Society in 1881 under Russian rule. They became the national flag in 1918; banned under Soviet rule from 1940, the flag flew again over Tallinn in 1989 and was restored by law in 1990. No law gives a meaning, but a popular reading from the poet Martin Lipp makes blue the sky, black the soil and the hard past, and white purity and hope.
fixes.value: Estonia's flag has three equal bands of blue, black and white, colors chosen by the Estonian Students' Society in 1881 under Russian rule. They became the national flag in 1918; banned under Soviet rule from 1940, the flag flew again over Tallinn in 1989 and was restored by law in 1990. No law gives a meaning, but a popular reading spread by the poet Martin Lipp makes blue the sky, black the soil of the homeland and white purity and hard work.
fixes.reason: The current last sentence attributes 'the hard past' and 'hope' to Martin Lipp's reading, which neither source does. Wikipedia's Flag of Estonia article gives the interpretation made popular by Lipp's poetry as blue for the sky, black for attachment to the soil of the homeland, and white for purity, hard work and commitment; Britannica gives sky, soil and aspiration toward freedom without naming Lipp. The prior pass's own doubt admitted 'hard past' was not Lipp's wording. The replacement keeps the hedged popular reading and matches what the sources attribute to Lipp. The 1881, 1918, 1940, 1989 and 1990 facts check against the Wikipedia article. 'No law gives a meaning' is kept rather than the verifier's 'The Flag Act gives no meaning' because the Riigi Teataja page returned no text when opened; Wikipedia states the Act sets only colour specifications. 447 characters, one paragraph, no jargon, American spelling.

fixes.current: Thomas Francis Meagher presented the three-band flag in 1848, inspired by the French flag. Officially, green stands for the older Gaelic and Catholic tradition and orange for the Protestant followers of William of Orange; the white between them, Meagher said, means a lasting truce between the two. It flew over Dublin's General Post Office in the 1916 Easter Rising, and the 1937 Constitution names it the national flag.
fixes.value: Thomas Francis Meagher presented the green, white and orange flag in 1848, inspired by the French flag. Green was the old color of Irish nationalists, orange that of the Protestant Orange Order named for William of Orange, and the white, Meagher said, means a lasting truce. Officially the flag means hoped-for union of the island's traditions. Flown over Dublin's General Post Office in the 1916 Easter Rising, it is named in the 1937 Constitution.
fixes.reason: Both verifiers flagged the word 'Officially' for the green = 'older Gaelic and Catholic tradition' reading, and I confirmed it against the Department of the Taoiseach's National Flag guidelines (September 2025 PDF, text extracted and read). The only meaning the government states is that the tricolour 'is intended to symbolise the inclusion and hoped-for union of the people of different traditions on this island'. It gives the colours' origins as history: the green flag with harp was 'an older symbol used by Irish nationalists', and the Orange Order, 'exclusively Protestant', was 'founded in 1795 in memory of King William of Orange'; it quotes only Meagher's 1848 line that the white 'signifies a lasting truce between Orange and Green'. 'Gaelic' appears nowhere in the official text, and the green = Catholics gloss appears only as an 1850 proposal and in Wikipedia's paraphrase of an older government page. The replacement states the documented origins plainly, gives the official meaning as official, keeps the verified 1848, 1916 and 1937 facts (all in the PDF), avoids 'tricolour', uses American spelling, no double quotes, and is 449 characters.

fixes.current: In 1917 a conference in Vilnius chose the colors. Red and green flags in the hall looked gloomy, so Tadas Daugirdas suggested adding yellow for the rising sun. The flag was adopted in 1918, banned under Soviet rule and restored in 1988. The flag law gives the colors no meaning, but yellow is often said to mean the sun and prosperity, green forests, freedom and hope, and red the blood and courage of those who died for Lithuania.
fixes.value: In 1917 a conference in Vilnius picked red and green, but red and green flags in the hall looked gloomy, so Tadas Daugirdas proposed adding yellow for the rising sun. The flag was adopted in 1918, banned under Soviet rule and restored in 1988. The flag law gives the colors no meaning, but yellow is often said to mean the sun and prosperity, green forests, freedom and hope, and red the blood and courage of those who died for Lithuania.
fixes.reason: The current opening sentence says the 1917 conference chose the colors (implying all three) and then says yellow was added afterwards, which contradicts itself. The Flag of Lithuania Wikipedia article (opened and checked) states that the 1917 Vilnius Conference delegates chose only two colors, green and red, found the red-green hall flags too dark and gloomy, and left the matter to a commission (Basanavicius, Zmuidzinavicius, Daugirdas) in which Daugirdas suggested adding a strip of yellow for the rising sun; the protocol went to the Council of Lithuania on 19 April 1918 and the flag was adopted in 1918. The replacement states that sequence correctly, keeps every other confirmed fact (1918 adoption, Soviet ban, 1988 restoration, law giving no meaning, hedged popular meanings), is 438 characters, one paragraph, American spelling, no jargon, no double quotes.

fixes.current: At the Battle of Laupen in 1339, Swiss soldiers sewed a white cross onto their clothing to tell friend from foe, and it became the shared sign of the old Swiss Confederacy. Why the background is red is debated: some say the blood of Christ, others the flag of Bern. The design was set for Swiss troops in 1841 and written into the constitution of 1848. The square shape comes from old war banners. The colors have no official meaning.
fixes.value: Swiss soldiers wore a white cross on their clothing at the Battle of Laupen in 1339, and it became the shared sign of the old Swiss Confederacy. Why the background is red is debated: some say the blood of Christ, others the flag of Bern. The design was set for Swiss troops in 1841; the 1848 constitution ordered it for all federal troops, and in 1889 it was confirmed as the federal emblem. No official meaning is given.
fixes.reason: Wikipedia (Flag of Switzerland): the 1848 constitution did not name a national flag; it only prescribed the federal flag for federal troops, and the Federal Council confirmed the design as the federal emblem in 1889. 'Written into the constitution of 1848' overstates it; the rest of the paragraph is kept. 422 characters.

fixes.current: Andorra has two heads of state at once, known as co-princes: the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the President of France.
fixes.value: Andorra's two co-princes are both foreign leaders: the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the President of France, under a power-sharing deal from 1278.
fixes.reason: Cross-batch repeat: San Marino's fun fact uses the identical hook 'has two heads of state at once'. Rewording Andorra keeps its unique fact (the 1278 Paréage between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix) and removes the duplicate phrasing. 150 characters. [Edited after review: "both outsiders" read as a judgement; "both foreign leaders" says the same fact plainly.]

fixes.current: Newgrange, a stone tomb in County Meath built around 3100 BC, is older than Stonehenge, and the winter solstice sunrise lights up its inner chamber.
fixes.value: Newgrange, a stone tomb in County Meath built around 3100 BC, was aligned so that the rising sun at the winter solstice lights up its inner chamber.
fixes.reason: Cross-batch repeat: Malta's fun fact already uses the 'older than Stonehenge' comparison (and adds the pyramids). Dropping it from Ireland leaves each country with its own hook; the solstice alignment is the better-known Newgrange fact. 148 characters.

ownerDecisions.issue: The field rule points to Wikipedia's list of countries by area, which prints 88,499 km2 for Serbia including its claim on Kosovo, while the app ships 77,589 km2 (the Serbia infobox figure excluding Kosovo, confirmed on the opened page) to match the owner rule that Serbia's population excludes Kosovo and to avoid double counting with the separate Kosovo entry; which convention applies is for the owner to confirm.

doubts.issue: The designer credit 'Mladen Kolobarić' appears only in Wikipedia's infobox without a citation; the flags-of-the-world page, the OHR decision and the OHR bulletin opened by the verifiers name no designer and say only that the flag was chosen from alternatives prepared by an expert commission, so the name is kept in the fix but could be dropped ('imposed this design') if the owner wants zero risk.

Maltese and English are the constitutional official languages; Maltese Sign Language is declared official only by the Maltese Sign Language Recognition Act 2016, so whether statutory sign languages belong in the list is an owner policy choice to apply consistently (same question as South Africa). No change proposed.

Constitution Article 13 makes Montenegrin the sole official language but says Serbian, Bosnian, Albanian and Croatian 'shall also be in the official use', and Wikipedia labels those four 'recognised national languages'; whether they belong in the list under the 'official or national languages' rule is a judgment call for the owner, and the current value is defensible.

The text says the colors are often said to mean peace and liberty but no law says so; the 2011 law and the coat of arms article give no color meaning, yet Wikipedia's flag article attributes white = peace and light blue = liberty to a San Marino government brochure (About the Republic of San Marino, esteri.sm). The hedge stays accurate, but the owner may prefer to state the basis as a government publication; the brochure itself was not opened, so no replacement is proposed.

Wikipedia's area list (the rule's source) gives 0.44 km2 total (land 0.44, water 0), so the shipped value follows the field rule, but the row's own footnote says the De Agostini Atlas corrected 0.44 to 0.49 km2 in 1945-46 and tags the 'official figure' claim as dubious, and the Vatican City article infobox gives 0.49 km2; the owner may prefer 0.49, so no fix is proposed.

Both the current and replacement text say Haiti's flag was identical at the 1936 Olympics; Wikipedia says it matched Haiti's civil flag, but a reader comment on the Flag Institute page claims the Haitian flag shown at the ceremony carried the coat of arms, so the exact circumstances of the clash rest on secondary accounts.

Wikipedia tags the claim that the Slovak white-blue-red design dates to 1848 as citation needed; Britannica confirms 1848-49 only for the redesigned arms, so the 1848 date for the bands rests on weaker sourcing than the rest of the text.

rejected.why: Second, near-identical proposal from the other verifier ('...and many of them still stand in fields, hills and beaches across the country'); merged into the single funFact fix above, which keeps 'small' and the decade range that both sources support.
The standalone doubt about 'raised this flag' and 'seal' is not reported separately because both points are resolved by the flagDescription fix above (coat of arms; a red flag with the eagle).

The shipped text is correct and verified: the national flag is square by law (Wikipedia flag article quoting the 2017 law; aboutswitzerland page says the square shape comes from square military banners). The mismatch is with the shipped image /tmp/flagwork/out/ch.png, which is 600 x 450 (4:3), an asset problem rather than a text error; the proposed sentence about boats flying a rectangular 2:3 version would not match a 4:3 picture either and adds detail the story does not need.
